candidate_windows.window_text: In this section, we elaborate RECoNNECT in detail. The core idea is to generate a direct explanation from the indirect documents. To achieve this, RECONNECT first expands the query as explanations for gathering more detailed documents from the external knowledge base (Section 3.1). With these documents,RECoNNECT stochastically samples the necessary knowledge to refine it into direct explanations for answering the question (Section 3.2). Finally, augmenting these refined explanations, RECONNECT predicts the answer during inference (Section 3.3). Figure 2 illustrates the overall procedure of the proposed framework.

We demonstrate the efficacy of RECoNNECT across diverse configurations of commonsense reasoning following these research questions:

Q1(Generalizability) Does RECoNNECT enable better performance than existing knowledge augmentation methods across diverse benchmarks? (\$4.4)

Q2 (Explainability) How does each component in RECoNNECT contribute to reasoning abilities of LLMs? $( \ S 4 . 5 , \ S 4 . 6 )$

Q3 (Insights) How direct explanations by RECONNECT improve the commonsense reasoning ability of LLMs? (\$4.7)

Language modelsConsistent with the previous work (Molfese et al., 2024), we use zero-shot settings for Llama 3.1-8B Instruct model (Grattafiori et al.,2O24) as our backbone.The further analysis for other LLMs is shown in Appendix E.

Retriever corpusWe build our retriever corpus by incorporating the RACo corpus and LLM-based QA datasets, including the ZEBRA (Molfese et al., 2024) and COCONUT corpus (Park et al., 2024). Specifically, we utilize only explanations from LLM-based QA datasets to unify different types of retrieval corpora. For a fair comparison, we use the same retrieval corpus for all baselines.Detailed implementations are shown in the Appendix A.2.

Retrieval modelsWe build our retriever based on E5-base-v2(Wang et al., 2022) (109M), which is pre-trained on a large corpus of text following the previous works (Molfese et al., 2024). We finetune the retriever on the training set of ZEBRAKB(Molfese et al., 2024) that contains diverse explanations generated by LLMs. We construct two explanations $e$ and $e ^ { \prime }$ as pair-wise positive if they explain the same questions.The details are shown in Appendix A.3

We compare our framework with two augmentation methods using the knowledge generated from LLMs or retrieved from an external corpus. Retrieval augmentationWe utilize retrievalaugmentation methods as baselines, which focus on augmenting relevant knowledge from commonsense corpora. We use commonsense retrieval augmentations as our baselines,such as RACo（Yu et al., 2022) and ZEBRA (Molfese et al., 2024). We additionally compare to advanced retrievalaugmentation methods, such as FLARE (Jiang et al., 2023) and DRAGIN(Su et al., 2024), which dynamically decide queries and retrieval timing in multi-round retrieval augmentation. Knowledge generationWe utilize the commonsense knowledge generation methods as baselines, which involve the generated knowledge from LLMs in an unsupervised manner, such as Self-Talk (Shwartz et al., 2020), GKP (Liu et al., 2022b), and supervised training, such as Rainier (Liu et al., 2022a), Crystal (Liu et al., 2023), and COCONUT (Park et al., 2O24) that require additional large training datasets and model for fine-tuning.

We perform ablation studies to verify the contributions of each component in RECoNNECT4.

Retrieval and generationAs shown in the upper part of Table 3,we observe that eliminating explanation-guided retrieval (ER) and knowledge connection (KC) negatively affects both ID and OOD datasets. Specifically, omitting knowledge connecting significantly hurts the performance by $3 . 7 \%$ and $4 . 3 \%$ on ID and OOD datasets, respectively. These results indicate that each component in our framework is essential to generate more highquality explanations.

Document sampling To validate the design choices for document sampling, we compared with three different subset sampling schemes: 1) Cluster sampling,which samples the documents from different clusters (Wang et al., 2025); 2) MMR sampling,which re-rank the samples to prevent redundancy and provide more diverse documents, 3) Top-K sampling,which selects $K$ documents that have the highest relevance score to their queries; 4) Random sampling，which samples the documents randomly. As shown in the lower part of Table 3,adopting random sampling substantially decreases both datasets,indicating the importance of constructing document subsets. Moreover, we observed that using either top- $K$ documents or semantically diverse documents from clusters to construct subsets exhibits inferior performance.These results support our design choice to sample the document subsets with diverse perspectives,while consisting of semantically relevant documents.

We provide detailed implementations, including hyperparameters, dataset statistics,retrieval model training,hardware details,and human evaluations.

We utilize ZEBRA-KB (Molfese et al., 2024) as our training corpus for retrieval models. Specifically, we utilize the questions and explanations for constructing training sets. We randomly split the training and test sets as $90 \%$ and $10 \%$ ,respectively. Following the previous work (Molfese et al., 2024), we select 64 positive samples for each explanation and use up to 2OO negative samples per batch. We set the maximum sequence lengths as 256 for questions and explanations,and train our models for 25K steps using RAdam (Liu et al., 202O). For learning rate and weight decay, we use le-5 and 1e-2, respectively.

We implement all baselines and our RECoNNECT using four RTX A6OOO GPUs for experiments. For all experiments, we implement with PyTorch, building on FlashAttention2 (Dao, 2024) and bfloat16 mixed-precision, to ensure efficient inference.
